headline: Swayne Field Shopping Center renovation nearing completion in Englewood — $3.6M federal investment targets workforce training anchor and minority-owned businesses
paragraphs: The Swayne Field Shopping Center in Toledo's Englewood neighborhood is nearing completion of a $3.6 million federally funded rehabilitation, The Blade reported May 26. The 92,000-square-foot, 7.4-acre facility is being redesigned from a car-centric strip center into a walkable plaza with green space, lighting, trees, landscaping including bioswales for stormwater management, and a complete facade update. A workforce training center is planned as the anchor tenant, alongside recruitment of small and minority-owned businesses.

The renovation is funded through $1.5 million in federal community project funds secured by U.S. Rep. Marcy Kaptur, a $1 million carryover in Community Development Block Grant funds, a $28,000 grant from the Toledo Community Foundation, and a Department of Energy Enhancement and Innovation Grant. A public arts commission call for integrated site artwork had a May 18, 2026 deadline, signaling the project is in its final pre-completion phase.

A pop-up produce market is opening at the Swayne Field site this fall as a food access pilot, 13abc reported August 26 and The Sojourner's Truth confirmed August 28. Al Peake & Sons — a Toledo-based food distributor with more than 75 years in business — will operate the market, handling sourcing, transportation, staffing, and food safety. The market opens September 4 and 5, then runs every Saturday through October 24 from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. at the corner of Monroe Street and Detroit Avenue. It will carry fresh Ohio- and Michigan-grown produce including herbs, leafy greens, vegetables, and fruits. The pilot is explicitly designed to expand affordable, healthy food access in a food-desert neighborhood — translating the Swayne Field redevelopment investment into an immediate food security benefit for residents who have limited access to full-service grocery retail.

The Blade reported August 31 that the market is designed to serve approximately 300 families per week, a figure the organizers set as the threshold for demonstrating sustained food access impact in Englewood. The grand opening runs September 4 (3–8 p.m.) and September 5 (10 a.m.–3 p.m.), with live demonstrations and community programming. A September 10 collaboration with a local art festival is also planned, integrating the market launch into broader neighborhood activation. Organizers described the goal as building a consistent weekly customer base before the Swayne Field retail anchor tenants — including the planned workforce training center — open in the renovation's next phase.

The Blade reported September 3, 2026 that the city of Toledo issued an apology over the way vendor outreach was conducted during the Swayne Field produce market rollout, acknowledging that the process could have been more inclusive and transparent for prospective small and minority-owned vendors who were interested in participating. City officials vowed to improve outreach procedures for future market and commercial opportunities tied to the Swayne Field site. The grand opening of the Swayne Market pop-up proceeded as scheduled: September 4 (3–8 p.m.) and September 5 (10 a.m.–3 p.m.) at Monroe Street and Detroit Avenue, operated by Al Peake & Sons with fresh Ohio- and Michigan-grown produce.
why_it_matters: Commercial corridor rehabilitation in legacy neighborhoods like Englewood mirrors the same thesis driving Vibrancy grants elsewhere in Toledo — federal and municipal anchor investment unlocks private tenant recruitment and neighborhood confidence. The workforce training center anchor is the highest-leverage piece: it seeds daily foot traffic independent of retail sales cycles and binds the site to workforce-development partners across the city. If Swayne Field's tenant mix stabilizes around the training center plus minority-owned storefronts, it becomes a replicable model for Toledo's other aging shopping plazas along Detroit, Alexis, and Sylvania Avenues that haven't seen recapitalization in decades.
